problem: Geometric semantic maps and 3D scene graphs (OK-Robot, HOVSG) rely on CLIP-style matching, are noisy and cannot interact with a VLM. Image-based topological methods (MobilityVLA) lack 3D structure and are slow at reasoning over long image sequences, so long-range object retrieval has low success and high latency.
motivation: Robots need persistent long-range spatial memory that supports both geometric grounding and VLM reasoning in large real indoor environments. Inspired by dual-process cognition, fast intuitive matching is cheap but error-prone, while VLM verification is accurate but slow, so combining them can give accuracy at lower latency.
key_idea: Build a four-level Hierarchical Multi-modal Scene Graph (floor/room/view/object) and use CLIP-based fast matching first, invoking VLM-based slow reasoning to verify and refine the goal view/object only when fast matching fails.
insight: Ablation (Table 3) shows that room-level spatial targets raise RSR@1m from 72.4 to 81.6, and adding slow navigation reasoning raises it further to 92.0, while costing 5.5s instead of 1.5s. Restricting VLM verification to candidate views rather than whole sequences cuts latency by 82% versus MobilityVLA and still gives higher accuracy.
method: HMSG: four-level graph (floor, room, view, object) with geometric, semantic (CLIP + VLM captions, GPT-4o room names) and topological features; built on the HOVSG instance-level open-vocabulary map from FAST-LIVO2 RGBD+pose.

View nodes: store CLIP embedding, VLM caption and camera pose, are linked to visible objects, and have undirected pose-based edges between views for path planning; each object is assigned its minimum-mean-depth view as its best view.
LLM instruction understanding: parses spatial instructions into floor/room/object components and infers goal objects for implicit instructions (e.g. 'I'm thirsty').
Fast matching: CLIP similarity between query text and view/object embeddings (within the named room if given) picks candidate goal view and object.

Slow reasoning: GPT-4o checks that the matched object is in its best view; if not, an LLM picks view-1 from the captions of unmatched views, the VLM compares view-1 with the fast-matched view, and the goal object is re-selected by CLIP similarity among that view's objects.
System integration: FunASR speech recognition, global path planning and whole-body control on a Unitree-G1 humanoid.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) for LLM/VLM reasoning + CLIP for matching
setting.observation: RGBD camera (RealSense D455) + Mid360 LiDAR with SLAM poses; pre-built map from a tour
setting.action_space: goal view/object coordinates passed to global path planner and whole-body control (retrieval evaluated, not low-level actions)
setting.simulator: real-world data; HM3D-SEM scenes for a secondary evaluation
setting.privileged: pre-exploration tour data to build the map offline; static environment assumed

numbers.eval_set_note: 87 crowd-sourced instructions over 4 self-collected humanoid tour datasets
numbers.extra: pre-built HMSG map; retrieval success only if the target is in the specified room; 5.5s avg time with slow reasoning

numbers_note: Values printed as fractions in tables were converted to percentages. Benchmarks are the paper's own retrieval sets (not standard VLN benchmarks); the split label 'test' is an approximation.
results: FSR-VLN reaches 92% SR (80/87) on the real-world retrieval set versus OK-Robot 60.9%, HOVSG 51.7%, and MobilityVLA 34.5%. It reduces response time by 82% versus MobilityVLA (5.5s vs 30s), and also beats HOVSG and osmAG-LLM on HM3D-SEM (RSR@Top1@1m 87% vs 52% and 28%).
limitations: HMSG construction is slow, so the approach is unsuitable for real-time mapping
Assumes a static environment and a pre-built map; no exploration

Evaluation is retrieval-only on a small self-collected set (87 instructions); the MobilityVLA baseline is a re-implementation with GPT-4o over 50 CLIP-preselected frames, and FSR-VLN is judged under a stricter room-specific criterion while baselines are judged more leniently
